newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korean zinc production seen plummeting.
newsitem.headline: North Korean zinc production seen plummeting.

text.p: North Korean zinc production is expected to continue sliding this year as the Stalinist nation struggles with serious shortages of electricity, ore and hard currency, traders in Tokyo said on Thursday.

"The situation in that country is catastrophic. They can't dig up ore because of the floods. They don't have enough electric power for supplying zinc refineries," said one trader. "The situation is going to last for a while."
Traders estimated zinc production in the famine-struck nation was running at about 1,500 tonnes a month, well below its annual output rate of some 80,000 tonnes a few years ago.
They said Pyongyang had no hard currency to acquire ore or electricity from other countries, such as neighbouring China, which has become an aggressive seller of the metal.

On Wednesday, traders in Seoul said a food-for-zinc barter arrangement between North Korea and U.S. grain giant Cargill Inc worth $4 million on each side was on the brink of falling apart because Pyongyang had not come up with the metal.
The deal with the commodities trading firm based in Minneapolis, Minnesota, would probably be the first direct American grain sale to North Korea since the Korean War ended in 1953.
Pyongyang has so far failed to deliver 4,000 tonnes of zinc which was to be paid for with 20,000 tonnes of Cargill grain.
"These things happen quite often with North Korea these days," said a zinc trader at a European trade house in Tokyo.
"We once sent a vessel to buy 500 tonnes of zinc, but there was only 150 tonnes. We won't be signing any contracts directly with North Korea under the current circumstances."

A trader at one of Japan's major trading house agreed, saying: "I saw North Korean zinc offered through Europe for a very low price recently. But we weren't sure if they were really going to deliver the metal."

Traders in Tokyo forecast North Korean 1997 zinc exports to Japan will stay low at around 7,000 tonnes after falling from more than 10,000 tonnes in 1995. In that year North Korea was the second-largest zinc exporter to Japan after China.

One official at a Tokyo trading house with close ties to North Korea said the main problem was that Pyongyang had to use zinc to pay for food from the United States, China and Taiwan after serious flooding for two years in a row.
"There's not enough zinc to sell to Japan," he said.
